title: 2 Kings 15:8–16
context: In Israel, Jeroboam II's son Zechariah reigns only six months before Shallum assassinates him, ending Jehu's dynasty in the fourth generation, as the LORD had told Jehu. Shallum himself lasts one month before Menahem kills him. Menahem then attacks Tiphsah when it will not open its gates. The passage begins Israel's final cascade of coups.

verses.text: In the thirty-eighth year of Azariah king of Judah, Zechariah the son of Jeroboam reigned over Israel in Samaria six months.
verses.arminianNotes: Zechariah, son of Jeroboam II, reigns six months in Samaria. Arminian readers note how abruptly a long and prosperous dynasty begins to collapse, a sign of instability that the following verses intensify.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Zechariah's brief reign comes in the thirty-eighth year of Azariah. The short notice marks the end of an era in Israel and the beginning of its rapid decline.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, as his fathers had done. He didn’t depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, with which he made Israel to sin.
verses.arminianNotes: He does evil and does not depart from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. Arminian readers note that he continues the national pattern of calf worship, choosing the familiar path rather than turning back to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the refrain about Jeroboam son of Nebat has followed nearly every northern king. The sin set at the kingdom's founding still shapes it near its end.

verses.text: Shallum the son of Jabesh conspired against him, and struck him before the people and killed him, and reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Shallum conspires against Zechariah and kills him "before the people." Arminian readers see the violence of a public assassination, a sign of how far the nation's order has broken down.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Hosea 8:4 describes this era: "They have set up kings, but not by me." Political violence replaces any seeking of God's will in choosing Israel's rulers.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Zechariah, behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Zechariah's acts are in the chronicles of the kings of Israel. Arminian readers note that six months leave little to record, and the writer moves quickly to what the end of his reign means.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator gives the standard closing formula even for so short a reign. Each king, however brief, is accounted for and measured against God's covenant.

verses.text: This was the LORD’s word which he spoke to Jehu, saying, “Your sons to the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel.” So it came to pass.
verses.arminianNotes: This fulfills the LORD's word to Jehu: "Your sons to the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel." Arminian readers note that God kept his promise exactly, no more and no less (2 Kings 10:30).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the narrator's direct comment: "So it came to pass." God's word governs the length of dynasties, and even an assassination fulfills what he spoke.

verses.text: Shallum the son of Jabesh began to reign in the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah king of Judah, and he reigned for a month in Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes: Shallum reigns one month in Samaria. Arminian readers note the irony that the man who seized the throne by violence holds it for only a month, a picture of how short-lived power gained this way can be.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Hosea 7:7 says, "All their kings have fallen. There is no one among them who calls to me." The rapid turnover shows a nation that has stopped seeking God.

verses.text: Menahem the son of Gadi went up from Tirzah, came to Samaria, struck Shallum the son of Jabesh in Samaria, killed him, and reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Menahem comes from Tirzah, kills Shallum, and reigns. Arminian readers see the cycle of violence continuing, each usurper overthrown by another in a pattern of freely chosen bloodshed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrative presents each coup in brief, repeated terms. The monotony of the language underlines the emptiness of a kingdom that has lost its anchor in God.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Shallum, and his conspiracy which he made, behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Shallum's acts and his conspiracy are recorded elsewhere. Arminian readers note that the writer names his conspiracy as the defining act of his brief reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Shallum's legacy is summed up as a conspiracy. A reign born in treachery leaves nothing else worth recording in the inspired account.

verses.text: Then Menahem attacked Tiphsah and all who were in it and its border areas, from Tirzah. He attacked it because they didn’t open their gates to him, and he ripped up all their women who were with child.
verses.arminianNotes: Menahem attacks Tiphsah because it did not open its gates, and the text says "he ripped up all their women who were with child." Arminian readers let the text's own words stand as a grave indictment of a king's cruelty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise take the verse as the narrator's sober record of atrocity, given without comment or detail. It shows how deeply violence has corrupted Israel's leadership in its last days.
